title: Post-quantize regression bisect plan
topics: KV cache interactions with quantized weights
INT8 vs FP8 vs GPTQ vs AWQ tradeoffs
summary: Customer observed a ~3-7% accuracy drift after switching to INT8-GPTQ pack for the 13B rec model in production. Team reviewed potential causes (quantization noise, KV cache misalignment, batch shape changes, nondeterministic seeds) and agreed on a bisect + controlled ablation plan. Redwood SE recommended mixed-precision canary, deterministic bisect harness, and synthetic latency/throughput runs on a VPC test cluster before any Dedicated capacity change. Next steps include running bisect tests across two eval sets, sharing failing prompts, and Redwood sending a playbook + test harness link.
action_items: Priya Shah - run bisect with 3 random seeds across EvalSet-A and EvalSet-B, include per-layer activations logging - due 2025-06-16
Jamal Ortiz - extract and upload 200 failing prompts + model config and seed details to shared drive - due 2025-06-14
Alex Mercer - send quantization playbook, benchmark template, and Dedicated capacity cost example (link) - due 2025-06-13
Sam Patel - provision VPC test cluster (2x A10g equivalent) and create access for Redwood SE - due 2025-06-18
next_steps: Schedule bisect results review (30 min) week of 2025-06-17
Run mixed-precision canary on small traffic slice if bisect inconclusive
If regression persists, run AWQ conversion for top-3 magnet layers and compare
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-06-12 14:00 UTC / Duration: 1h18m / Recording id: ff-20250612-9a3b2c
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jamal Ortiz (NeuraShop ML), Nora Chen (NeuraShop Head ML), Sam Patel (NeuraShop Infra)
Shared links: playbook: https://redwood.example/quant-playbook (placeholder), bench spreadsheet: https://drive.example/neural-bench (placeholder)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick roll call, and then Priya will dive in. Jamal, Nora, Sam -- can you confirm you can see the screen?
[00:10] Jamal: Yep, all good. Audio's fine. Thanks for setting this up.
[00:15] Nora: Hi, thanks. We're pretty concerned about the drop we saw after the INT8 rollout.
[00:20] Priya: Cool. Quick agenda: first, recap symptoms and what you saw in prod; second, go through candidate causes and a controlled bisect plan; third, perf implications and VPC test plan. Sound good?
[00:28] Jamal: Sounds good. I'll start with the symptom. So we rolled the 13B rec model from FP16 to an INT8-GPTQ pack last week. Latency improved about 12% median, cost drops around 30%, but our top-k recall on the personalization eval dropped ~3-7% depending on the slice. It's subtle but impactful to conversions.
[00:47] Alex: When you say top-k recall, is that on offline eval or live A/B?
[00:50] Jamal: Offline first, based on our pre-computed holdout sets. We also saw a small signal in the 1% live canary which triggered the rollback.
[00:58] Priya: Got it. A couple immediate hypotheses: quantization rounding noise in crucial layers, KV cache mismatch when passing past key/values between segments, batch shape distribution change causing different attention casting, or something nondeterministic like RNG seeds during GPTQ conversion.
[01:18] Sam: I also want to flag infra changes — we moved the VPC egress rules at the same time, but that should be unrelated to model outputs. Still, I want to make sure nothing in serialization changed.
[01:30] Priya: Good call. Often infra changes are red herrings but we check. Another weird one we've seen is a mismatch between the tokenization preprocessor versions that coincides with quantize commits.
[01:40] Nora: We pinned tokenizers but we'll double-check. Jamal, could you share the conversion script and flags?
[01:45] Jamal: Yes. We used the standard GPTQ pack flow, with per-channel quantization, clipping threshold at 3.0, and we fused adjacent linear layers. I can upload the exact script.
[01:56] Priya: Helpful. Two immediate tests I recommend: 1) a bisect across layers to find which layer(s) amplify reconstruction error, and 2) a deterministic inference pass where we disable KV caching and force fixed batch shapes to rule out batching effects.
[02:12] Alex: And as part of the bisect, Priya suggested running both INT8 and AWQ on the top candidates to see if alternative quant schemes trade accuracy for throughput.
[02:22] Jamal: AWQ from your previous notes is promising but we were worried about speed. Does AWQ add runtime overhead?
[02:28] Priya: Slightly, AWQ's codepath in our runtime can be a bit heavier per-token for some kernels, but on the right hardware the throughput is comparable if you tune batching. FP8 is another axis; FP8 usually preserves more fidelity but increases memory and may affect batching constraints.
[02:44] Sam: On hardware, we run on A10g for prod now. Priya, does Redwood have perf numbers for AWQ on A10g vs INT8-GPTQ?
[02:52] Priya: We have internal numbers; I'll send the sheet. Roughly, INT8-GPTQ often has the best cost/perf for 13B on A10g, AWQ can be close for latency-sensitive slice if you keep batch size small and use mixed precision for attention. But that's pretty workload dependent.
[03:08] Jamal: Okay. The challenge is the production slices where accuracy matters most are low-latency and small-batch, so if AWQ hurts latency it's a non-starter.
[03:18] Priya: Understood. That's why the bisect should include latency probes at each step — we won't just look at quality; we'll measure median and p95 with the KV cache enabled and disabled.
[03:29] Nora: You mentioned KV cache mismatch earlier. Can you explain how quantization could affect cached keys/values? That seems odd to me.
[03:36] Priya: Sure. Two things: one, if quantization changes the numeric stability of attention outputs slightly, those differences can propagate into the KV cache and amplify over long contexts; two, if there's any off-by-one or dtype conversion when serializing the cache between segments, rounding differences can be introduced. We've seen a case where the runtime serialized the cache as float16 in one path and float32 in another after a quantize change.
[04:00] Sam: That sounds plausible — our cache serializer had a fallback to fp16 for network transfer. I'll check the service logs for any dtype conversion.
[04:07] Alex: To make this actionable, Priya proposed a three-pronged bisect: layer-level ablation, quant-scheme swap (INT8->AWQ->FP8), and caching toggles. We want to run on two eval sets: EvalSet-A (2000 examples, real traffic distribution) and EvalSet-B (focused edge cases you sent last week).
[04:28] Jamal: Yes, EvalSet-B contains the tricky personalization tails.
[04:33] Priya: Good. For the bisect harness: we'll run deterministic seeds (seed list of 3), log per-layer reconstruction MSE, attention output L2 on a fixed batch shape, and capture latency p50/p95 with the same concurrency as prod canary (concurrency 8). We'll produce a delta report per experiment.
[04:56] Nora: How long will that take to run?
[04:58] Priya: On a single test cluster with 2x A10g equiv, each full sweep (all layers ablated one by one) will take roughly 6-8 hours for EvalSet-A with the extra logging. With parallelization across two nodes we can bring it down to ~3-4 hours. That's why we asked Sam to provision the VPC test cluster.
[05:16] Sam: I'll start provisioning after this call. I can also snapshot current prod infra to avoid divergence.
[05:21] Alex: Great. A couple of practical notes: please keep the bisect runs isolated network-wise — don't reuse the prod KV cache — and use Redwood's test harness container we shared in the playbook link. Jamal, you said you'll upload the failing prompts?
[05:34] Jamal: Yes, I'll upload 200 worst offenders and also a random 2k sample for context.
[05:40] Priya: Perfect. Another debugging trick: run the GPipe-style step where you quantize everything but keep the attention softmax in FP16 to see if the error is localized to attention calculations.
[05:50] Nora: That's a neat idea. If attention is the culprit we could consider mixed-precision attention while keeping feed-forwards in INT8.
[05:58] Jamal: Would that require a custom build of the runtime?
[06:02] Priya: Not necessarily. Our runtime supports per-op dtype overrides in the config; we can run a canary with attention FP16 and the rest INT8. It's slightly slower but a clear ablation.
[06:12] Alex: On the topic of metric drift detection, do you want Redwood to set up continuous regression alerts tied to these eval sets? If the canary triggers again we can auto-fallback to FP16 or the previous pack.
[06:22] Nora: Yes, automated fallback would be great. We want to avoid manual rollbacks during peak times.
[06:27] Priya: We can configure fallback rules: if relative change in top-k recall > 2% on EvalSet-A in a 1h window, automatically switch traffic to the previous model for a rolling minute and alert the team. We will draft the rule.
[06:41] Jamal: That automation is good. One thing we worry about is nondeterministic seeds in GPTQ conversion producing subtly different packs. Should we enforce a fixed seed in conversion and store the seed in model metadata?
[06:53] Priya: Absolutely. The pack should include metadata: conversion seed, quant library version, clipping params, and a hash of the original FP16 weights. That way you can reproduce exactly. We'll include that in the playbook.
[07:05] Sam: Regarding VPC/on-prem: if we run the tests on-prem, log shipping is a pain. Is it better to run via Redwood Private or replicate locally?
[07:13] Alex: For debugging we prefer a Redwood Private test cluster attached to your VPC via a transient peering setup. That keeps logs centralized while maintaining data residency. We can do a short-term peering with limited access.
[07:25] Nora: Sounds good. Cost question: if we move to mixed-precision canary with Dedicated, what sort of cost delta might we see?
[07:33] Alex: I'll send a sample pricing snapshot. Generally mixed precision increases memory usage a bit, possibly needing a higher instance size for peak throughput; that leads to a modest bump in reserved capacity cost but may be offset by reduced rollback risks.
[07:46] Priya: Back to the technical plan: step 1, deterministic bisect with layer ablation on both eval sets. Step 2, run quant-scheme swaps (INT8->AWQ->FP8) on top candidate layers. Step 3, toggle KV cache and run a small online canary to validate. We'll capture per-layer deltas, latency p50/p95, and throughput.
[08:07] Jamal: If we find a single layer causing most drift, can we apply mixed-precision only to that layer in prod?
[08:12] Priya: Yes, that's a common mitigation: keep problematic layers in FP16 or FP8 and quantize the rest. The runtime supports per-layer dtype overrides via model config.
[08:21] Nora: Okay, let's run it. Timeline constraints: we prefer a remediation before our next feature push on 2025-06-24.
[08:28] Alex: That gives us two weeks. Action items we'll circulate. Priya, are you comfortable owning the bisect harness run with Sam's infra help?
[08:36] Priya: Yes. I'll coordinate with Sam on access and with Jamal on data uploads.
[08:40] Jamal: I'll also include the tokenizer version and conversion script.
[08:44] Alex: Great. Quick recap of next steps and owners... (recap) Priya runs bisect, Jamal uploads prompts and scripts, Sam provisions VPC test cluster, Alex sends playbook and pricing. We'll meet for a 30-min sync week of 2025-06-17 to review results.
[08:58] Nora: Thanks, everyone. This was helpful.
[09:02] Alex: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with links and the scheduled review.

End of transcript.
